Level 1: Cleaning with soap and water. It gets the dirt and some germs off. It is the first step, not the last.
Level 2: The lowest level of infection control. It removes visible dirt and lowers the number of germs, but it does not kill all of them.
Level 3: The first level of infection control. Washing with soap or detergent and water removes debris and reduces germs so that a disinfectant can work afterward.
Level 4: Level one of infection control. Clean with soap or detergent and water before you disinfect, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt and oil.

Level 1: Using a strong germ-killing liquid on tools after you clean them. It kills almost all germs.
Level 2: The middle level. An EPA-registered disinfectant kills most bacteria, viruses and fungi on hard, nonporous tools. It does not kill bacterial spores.
Level 3: The second level of infection control. A chemical disinfectant registered with the EPA destroys most pathogens on nonporous surfaces, though bacterial spores survive. Tools must be cleaned first.
Level 4: The salon standard for tools that touch clients. Clean first, then keep the tool wet with an EPA-registered disinfectant for the full contact time on the label. Never used on skin.

Level 1: Killing every single germ, even the toughest ones. Doctors' offices do this.
Level 2: The highest level. It destroys all microbes, including bacterial spores, usually with an autoclave that uses steam and pressure.
Level 3: The highest level of infection control. It destroys every microorganism, including spores, most often with an autoclave. It is required for tools that puncture the skin.
Level 4: Kills all microbial life. Needed for anything that breaks the skin, like a lancet. Most salons use single-use disposables for those instead and throw them away.

Level 1: How long the germ-killing liquid has to stay wet on something before it works.
Level 2: The amount of time a disinfectant must stay wet on a surface to kill the germs listed on its label.
Level 3: The period a surface must stay visibly wet with disinfectant for the product to work as its label claims. A shorter time means the tool is not disinfected.
Level 4: The wet time the label requires. Wiping a tool dry early means it is not disinfected, and an inspector can cite you for it.

Level 1: Tiny living things you can't see. Most are harmless. The 'pathogenic' kind makes people sick.
Level 2: One-celled microorganisms. Nonpathogenic bacteria are harmless or helpful. Pathogenic bacteria cause disease.
Level 3: Single-celled organisms that cause disease when they enter the body. They are a minority among bacteria; nonpathogenic types are harmless or useful.
Level 4: Most bacteria are harmless. The disease-causing kind are the reason every infection control rule exists.

Level 1: A tiny germ that can only grow inside living cells. Cold sores come from a virus.
Level 2: A germ smaller than bacteria that can only multiply inside a host's cells. Examples: herpes simplex (cold sores), hepatitis B and HIV.
Level 3: An infectious particle that reproduces only by taking over a host's cells. Viral infections such as herpes simplex and hepatitis are not cured by antibiotics.
Level 4: Cannot live or multiply without a host. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. An active cold sore means no service in that area.

Level 1: Germs like mold and yeast. Ringworm is a fungus, not a worm.
Level 2: Molds, mildews and yeasts. Tinea, also called ringworm, is a contagious fungal skin infection.
Level 3: Organisms such as molds and yeasts. Tinea is a contagious fungal infection of the skin that forms itchy, ring-shaped patches, and it is a reason to refuse service on that area.
Level 4: Tinea shows up as a red, scaly ring. It is contagious, so do not service the area. Refer the client to a doctor.

Level 1: Treat everyone's blood like it could have germs. Every client, every time.
Level 2: Guidelines that say to treat all blood and body fluids as if they could be infectious, and to wear gloves and other protection.
Level 3: Infection control guidelines that require treating all human blood and certain body fluids as potentially infectious, using gloves and protective equipment with every client.
Level 4: Assume any client could carry a bloodborne disease. Gloves, disposables and the blood exposure steps every time. Never judge who 'looks sick.'

Level 1: If a client gets cut: stop, put on gloves, clean it, cover it, and bag anything with blood on it.
Level 2: Stop the service, put on gloves, clean the area with antiseptic, cover it with a bandage, double-bag blood-soiled items, then disinfect tools and surfaces.
Level 3: The set of steps followed when blood appears during a service: stop, put on gloves, clean and cover the wound, double-bag contaminated items, and disinfect tools and surfaces before continuing.
Level 4: Stop. Glove up. Clean and apply antiseptic. Bandage. Double-bag the waste. Disinfect tools and the station. Remove gloves and wash hands. It is a full scored section of the practical exam.

Level 1: A paper that tells you how a product could hurt you and what to do if it does.
Level 2: A document from the manufacturer listing a product's ingredients, hazards, safe handling, storage and first aid.
Level 3: A standardized document the manufacturer supplies for each chemical product. It explains hazards, safe handling and storage, protective equipment and emergency first aid.
Level 4: Every chemical product in the salon needs one. It covers hazards, protective gear, storage and first aid. Know where your salon keeps them.

Level 1: The top layer of your skin. It is the part you can see and touch.
Level 2: The outermost layer of skin. It has no blood vessels and renews itself as new cells move up from the bottom.
Level 3: The thin outer layer of the skin. It contains no blood vessels and is made of several layers of cells that form at the bottom and move upward until they shed.
Level 4: The outer layer, with no blood vessels. New cells form in the basal layer at the bottom and rise to the surface, where they shed.

Level 1: The very top of the top skin layer. It is made of flat, dead cells that flake off.
Level 2: The outermost layer of the epidermis. Dead cells filled with keratin that protect the body and shed all the time.
Level 3: The top layer of the epidermis, made of flattened, keratin-filled dead cells. It forms the skin's protective barrier and is the layer that exfoliation treatments remove.
Level 4: This is the skin's barrier, and it is what exfoliation removes. Over-exfoliating damages it and makes skin sensitive.

Level 1: The thick layer under the top skin. It has blood, nerves, oil glands and hair roots.
Level 2: The 'true skin' under the epidermis. It holds blood vessels, nerves, sweat and oil glands, hair follicles, collagen and elastin.
Level 3: The thicker layer beneath the epidermis. It supplies the skin with blood and nerves and contains collagen for strength and elastin for flexibility.
Level 4: The support layer. Collagen keeps skin firm and elastin lets it bounce back. Sun and age break both down, which causes wrinkles.

Level 1: The fat layer under the skin. It keeps you warm and works like a cushion.
Level 2: Also called the hypodermis. Fatty tissue under the dermis that cushions, insulates and stores energy.
Level 3: The layer of fatty tissue below the dermis, also called the hypodermis. It cushions the body, holds in heat and stores energy.
Level 4: The fat layer under the dermis. It gets thinner with age, which adds to sagging.

Level 1: The coloring in your skin. More melanin means darker skin, and it helps block the sun.
Level 2: The pigment made by melanocytes that gives skin and hair color and protects against UV rays.
Level 3: Pigment produced by cells called melanocytes in the lowest layer of the epidermis. It determines skin color and absorbs UV radiation to protect the cells.
Level 4: Made in the basal layer. Too much in one spot is hyperpigmentation and too little is hypopigmentation. Skin with more melanin darkens more easily after irritation.

Level 1: Tiny glands in the skin that make oil.
Level 2: Oil glands attached to hair follicles. They release sebum, which keeps skin and hair soft.
Level 3: Oil glands connected to hair follicles. They secrete sebum, which lubricates the skin; too much sebum leads to oily skin and clogged follicles.
Level 4: They make sebum. Overactive glands mean oily skin and clogged pores, mostly in the T-zone.

Level 1: A clogged pore. Blackheads and whiteheads are both comedones.
Level 2: A hair follicle plugged with oil and dead cells. An open comedone is a blackhead. A closed comedone is a whitehead.
Level 3: A follicle blocked by sebum and dead cells. It is open (a blackhead) when the plug reaches the surface and oxidizes, and closed (a whitehead) when skin covers it.
Level 4: A blackhead is dark because the oil oxidizes in air, not because of dirt. Extract only on softened skin, wearing gloves.

Level 1: A papule is a small red bump. A pustule is a bump with pus in it.
Level 2: Both are primary lesions. A papule is a small raised bump with no fluid. A pustule is raised and contains pus.
Level 3: Two primary lesions seen in acne. A papule is a solid, raised, inflamed bump; a pustule is a similar bump that contains pus.
Level 4: Know the main lesions: macule is a flat spot like a freckle, papule is a bump with no pus, pustule is a bump with pus, and vesicle is a small blister of clear fluid.

Level 1: A skin problem that makes the cheeks and nose red and easy to irritate.
Level 2: A long-lasting inflammatory condition with redness, visible blood vessels and sometimes bumps in the center of the face.
Level 3: A chronic inflammatory condition of the central face marked by flushing, visible capillaries and sometimes bumps. Heat and stimulation make it worse, so treatments must be gentle.
Level 4: Triggered by heat, sun, spicy food and alcohol. Skip heat, steam and harsh scrubs. You can soothe the skin, but only a doctor diagnoses and treats it.

Level 1: A checklist for moles that could be dangerous: shape, edges, color, size and change.
Level 2: A guide to spotting melanoma: Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter, Evolving.
Level 3: A screening guide for melanoma: Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Color, Diameter over 6 mm, and Evolving. An esthetician who notices these signs refers the client to a physician.
Level 4: Uneven shape, ragged border, more than one color, wider than a pencil eraser (6 mm), or changing over time. Never diagnose. Refer to a dermatologist.

Level 1: The growing stage of hair.
Level 2: The active growth phase of the hair cycle. It is the best time to remove hair because the hair is still attached at the root.
Level 3: The first and longest stage of the hair growth cycle, when the hair is actively growing and anchored in the follicle. Hair removed in this stage takes longest to return.
Level 4: Growth phase, when hair removal works best. The cycle goes anagen (growing), then catagen (changing), then telogen (resting and shedding).

Level 1: A number from 0 to 14 that tells how sour (acid) or soapy (alkaline) something is. 7 is in the middle.
Level 2: Measures acidity and alkalinity. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. Healthy skin is slightly acidic, about 4.5 to 5.5.
Level 3: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or alkaline a substance is. Seven is neutral; the skin's surface normally measures about 4.5 to 5.5, which is mildly acidic.
Level 4: Skin works best around 4.5 to 5.5. Highly alkaline products, like harsh bar soap, strip the skin and leave it tight and irritated.

Level 1: A thin, slightly sour layer on top of the skin that protects it from germs.
Level 2: A protective film of oil and sweat on the skin's surface. It is slightly acidic and helps keep bacteria out.
Level 3: The thin, slightly acidic film of sebum and sweat on the skin's surface. It slows bacterial growth and helps the skin hold moisture.
Level 4: A film of sebum and sweat that keeps bacteria down and moisture in. Over-cleansing destroys it.

Level 1: Oil and water mixed together so they stay mixed, like lotion.
Level 2: A mix of two liquids that normally don't blend, like oil and water, held together by an emulsifier.
Level 3: A stable blend of oil and water made possible by an emulsifier. Most creams and lotions are emulsions, either oil-in-water or water-in-oil.
Level 4: Oil-in-water is lighter, like lotion. Water-in-oil is heavier, like cold cream. Emulsifiers keep the mixture from separating.

Level 1: Talking with the client before the service to learn about their skin and health.
Level 2: The conversation and intake form before a service: health history, medications, allergies, skin concerns and goals.
Level 3: The discussion and written intake completed before a service. It gathers health history, medications, allergies and goals so the esthetician can choose a safe treatment.
Level 4: Every service starts here. Review the intake form, ask about medications and recent treatments, check for contraindications, and write it all down.

Level 1: Covering the client with a towel and head wrap to keep them clean and comfortable.
Level 2: Protecting the client's hair and clothes with a head wrap and body drape before a service.
Level 3: Covering the client's hair and clothing with clean linens before a service. It protects the client and keeps the work area sanitary.
Level 4: The head drape keeps hair off the face, and the body drape protects clothes and privacy. Examiners check it as part of client protection.

Level 1: A reason you should NOT do a treatment on someone.
Level 2: A condition that means a service should not be done because it could harm the client.
Level 3: Any condition, medication or recent treatment that makes a service unsafe for a particular client. The esthetician must change or refuse the service.
Level 4: Stop and don't proceed if you see a contagious condition, open sores, a sunburn, recent isotretinoin (Accutane) use before waxing or peels, or a pacemaker before electrical treatments. When in doubt, ask for a doctor's release.

Level 1: A chart from I to VI that sorts skin by how easily it burns or tans.
Level 2: Classifies skin into Types I to VI by how it reacts to the sun, from 'always burns' (I) to 'never burns' (VI).
Level 3: A six-type classification of skin based on its response to UV exposure. It helps predict the risk of burning and of pigment changes after treatment.
Level 4: Higher types have more risk of dark spots after peels or irritation, so go gentler on them.

Level 1: Skin type is what you were born with. Skin condition is how your skin is acting right now.
Level 2: Skin type (dry, normal, combination, oily) is genetic. Skin condition (dehydrated, sensitive, acne-prone) can change over time.
Level 3: Skin type is inherited and based mainly on oil production. Skin conditions, such as dehydration or sensitivity, develop from outside and internal factors and can be improved.
Level 4: You can't change the type, but you treat the condition. Analysis under a magnifying lamp decides the treatment plan.

Level 1: A special purple light that shows things about the skin you can't see in normal light.
Level 2: A filtered UV light used in skin analysis. Different skin conditions glow different colors under it.
Level 3: A filtered ultraviolet lamp used in a darkened room during skin analysis. Conditions such as pigmentation, oiliness and dehydration show up as different colors.
Level 4: Used in a dark room with the client's eyes covered. Shows hidden pigmentation, dehydration, oil and product buildup.

Level 1: Getting dead skin off the top. You can scrub it off, or use a product that loosens it.
Level 2: Mechanical exfoliation uses friction (scrubs, brushes, microdermabrasion). Chemical exfoliation uses acids or enzymes.
Level 3: Two ways to remove dead cells from the stratum corneum. Mechanical methods physically rub or scrape them away; chemical methods dissolve the bonds that hold them together.
Level 4: Mechanical means scrubs, microdermabrasion and dermaplaning. Chemical means AHAs, BHAs and enzymes. Never exfoliate over infection or sunburn, or on a client using isotretinoin.

Level 1: Two kinds of skin acids. AHA works on the surface. BHA gets down into oily pores.
Level 2: AHAs (glycolic, lactic) dissolve in water and work on the surface. BHA (salicylic) dissolves in oil and gets into pores, so it helps acne.
Level 3: Two families of exfoliating acids. Alpha hydroxy acids are water-soluble and smooth the surface; beta hydroxy acid (salicylic) is oil-soluble and clears the inside of the pore.
Level 4: AHA for dullness and aging skin. BHA for oily and acne-prone skin. Salicylic acid is related to aspirin, so ask about aspirin allergies first.

Level 1: Slow, gentle stroking in massage. Used to start and end the massage.
Level 2: A light, gliding massage stroke used to begin, connect and end a massage and relax the client.
Level 3: A soft, continuous stroking movement made with the fingers or palms. It soothes the client and is used to begin and end a facial massage.
Level 4: The other strokes are petrissage (kneading), tapotement (tapping), friction and vibration. Effleurage opens and closes.

Level 1: Kneading the skin, like squeezing dough.
Level 2: A kneading movement that lifts and squeezes the tissue to boost circulation.
Level 3: A kneading movement that lifts, rolls and squeezes the tissue. It stimulates circulation and the deeper layers of the skin.
Level 4: A deeper, stimulating stroke. Avoid it on sensitive or rosacea skin.

Level 1: Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
Level 2: A fast tapping or light slapping movement. It is the most stimulating massage stroke.
Level 3: A rapid tapping movement, also called percussion. It is the most stimulating massage technique and is used sparingly.
Level 4: The most stimulating movement there is. Not for sensitive or reactive skin.

Level 1: A machine with a glass tube that glows and helps kill acne germs.
Level 2: An electrical device that uses a glass electrode. It warms the skin and kills germs. In the direct method it touches the skin. In the indirect method the client holds it.
Level 3: A device that sends a rapidly alternating current through a glass electrode. It produces heat and has a germ-killing effect, which makes it useful after extractions.
Level 4: Direct is antibacterial and is used after extractions. Indirect means the client holds the electrode while you massage. Avoid with pacemakers, metal implants, pregnancy or epilepsy.

Level 1: A machine that uses a small, steady electric current to clean out pores or push products in.
Level 2: A direct current with a negative and a positive pole. Desincrustation softens oil in pores, and iontophoresis pushes products into the skin.
Level 3: A constant direct current used for two treatments: desincrustation, which softens sebum in the follicles, and iontophoresis, which carries water-soluble products into the skin.
Level 4: The negative pole is alkaline: it softens sebum (desincrustation). The positive pole is acidic: it firms and soothes. Same no-go list as other electrical treatments.

Level 1: A machine that sands off dead skin with tiny crystals or a rough tip, then vacuums it up.
Level 2: Mechanical exfoliation using crystals or a diamond tip plus suction to remove dead surface cells.
Level 3: A form of mechanical exfoliation that uses crystals or a diamond tip with vacuum suction to remove surface cells. It is not used on inflamed or broken skin.
Level 4: A New Mexico practical add-on, done on the forehead in 10 minutes. Hold the skin taut, use even passes, and avoid pustules and the eye area.

Level 1: Something you spread on the face and leave on. Clay masks soak up oil. Cream masks add moisture.
Level 2: Clay or mud absorbs oil, gel soothes and hydrates, cream moisturizes, rubberized seals in serum, and thermal (paraffin) warms.
Level 3: Masks are selected by skin need: clay draws out oil, cream adds moisture, gel calms and hydrates, modeling (rubberized) masks seal in products, and paraffin holds in heat.
Level 4: Choose by skin: clay for oily, cream for dry, gel for sensitive or red, rubberized to lock in serums, and paraffin for warmth. Keep paraffin away from rosacea.

Level 1: Soft wax needs a cloth strip to pull it off. Hard wax hardens, and you pull it off by itself.
Level 2: Soft wax goes on thin and comes off with a strip. Hard wax goes on thicker, hardens, and comes off without a strip, so it is gentler on the face.
Level 3: Two depilatory waxes. Soft wax is spread thinly and removed with a strip; hard wax sets on the skin and is lifted off without one, which suits sensitive areas.
Level 4: Soft wax goes on in the direction of hair growth and comes off against it, quickly, with the skin held taut. Hard wax grips hair, not skin. Never wax over retinoids, Accutane or a recent peel.

Level 1: Putting a used stick back into the wax pot. Never do it.
Level 2: Reusing an applicator in the wax pot, which contaminates the wax.
Level 3: Placing a used applicator back into a product such as wax. It transfers bacteria into the container and violates infection control rules.
Level 4: One stick, one dip. Double-dipping spreads bacteria to every client after you, and it is a sanitation violation.

Level 1: Colors across from each other on the color wheel cancel each other out. Green hides red.
Level 2: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel and neutralize each other. Green covers redness, and peach covers blue-purple circles.
Level 3: Using complementary colors, which sit opposite each other on the color wheel, to neutralize discoloration before foundation. Green offsets red; peach offsets blue.
Level 4: Green over redness, yellow over purple, peach or orange over blue dark circles, and lavender over sallow skin. Correct first, then apply foundation.

Level 1: Resting your hand on the client's face so you stay steady near the eyes.
Level 2: Supporting your working hand on the client's face for control when working near the eyes or lips.
Level 3: Steadying the working hand against the client's face. It gives control and prevents injury when applying products near the eyes and mouth.
Level 4: Keeps your hand steady during liner, lip, brow and lash work. It is checked for safety on the practical exam.

Level 1: Gluing a strip of fake lashes onto the client's lash line.
Level 2: Applying a full band of artificial lashes with adhesive right along the natural lash line.
Level 3: Attaching a band of artificial lashes along the natural lash line with adhesive. The band is measured and trimmed to fit before it is applied.
Level 4: Trim the band to fit the eye, let the glue get tacky, then set it at the lash line from the center out. A New Mexico practical add-on: both eyes in 10 minutes.

Level 1: The list of things your license lets you do, and the things it doesn't.
Level 2: The services a New Mexico esthetician may legally do, such as facials, makeup, lash and brow tinting, and most hair removal.
Level 3: The services a license legally permits. New Mexico estheticians perform skin care, makeup, lash and brow services and non-invasive hair removal, but nothing invasive or medical.
Level 4: Facials, skin treatments, light therapy, high frequency, makeup, lash extensions, lash and brow tint, and hair removal except electrolysis, invasive methods and shaving. You can't call yourself a 'medical esthetician.'

Level 1: The number of school hours you need before you can take the license test.
Level 2: New Mexico requires 600 hours at a licensed school: 125 theory, 75 sanitation, 350 facials and 50 business.
Level 3: The training New Mexico requires before the licensing exams. The hours are divided among theory, infection control, facials and salon business.
Level 4: 600 hours finished within the past 24 months, then three exams. Theory is now 125 hours after the January 2026 rule change.

Level 1: You need at least a 70 on each of the three tests to pass.
Level 2: Each part (NIC theory, NIC practical and NM state law) needs a scaled score of 70 or higher.
Level 3: The minimum scaled score New Mexico requires on each of the three licensing exams. Each exam is scored separately.
Level 4: Lowered from 75 to 70 in January 2026. Pass each part separately; passing one doesn't make up for another.

Level 1: The state group that gives out esthetician licenses in New Mexico.
Level 2: The New Mexico board, part of the Regulation and Licensing Department, that licenses estheticians and enforces the rules in 16.34 NMAC.
Level 3: The state agency that licenses and regulates estheticians. It writes the rules in 16.34 NMAC, inspects establishments and can discipline licensees.
Level 4: Issues and renews licenses, inspects salons, and disciplines violations. Its rules live in Title 16, Chapter 34 of the New Mexico Administrative Code.
